presenceLabel: Miami, Wea or Piankashaw town, hunting area or cession here
presenceNote: Miami, Wea and Piankashaw are divisions of one people (Myaamia). The nation is shown c.1654–1846: medium confidence for the town points, low–medium for the county tints. Their villages were on the Wabash and earlier around Lake Michigan, all north of the Ohio; northern Kentucky was hunting ground from the mid-1700s. The hunters story is shown as c.1750–1795 (low confidence); the Piankashaw story is the 1804 cession. No Kentucky area is drawn: the sources give no boundary.
overlapNote: The 1804 tract is also the Delaware cession: the Piankashaw said they gave it to the Delawares c.1768, the Miami said the Delawares only had leave to occupy it, and the 1805 treaty resolved it. Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot and Mingo hunted the same northern Kentucky country (Henderson). Kickapoo and Mascouten lived beside the Wea and Piankashaw.
basis: Treaty texts (Piankeshaw 1804, Delaware 1804, Grouseland 1805, Greenville 1795), NPS page reproducing Royce's 1881 Indiana key, Indiana DNR, Miami Tribe of Oklahoma history, Kreinbrink (NKyTribune). County list for the 1804 cession approximates the treaty line.

eras.label: c.1654–1717 · Wisconsin, Lake Michigan and Detroit
eras.text: Wikipedia’s account of the Miami (after Kubiak, Tanner and Rafert) has them on the Fox River, Wisconsin, in 1654 and the Wisconsin River in 1670–95; at Niles, Michigan, in 1673; on the St. Joseph River, Michigan, in 1679–81; at Chicago in 1680; at Starved Rock, Illinois, in 1682; on the Calumet River in 1687; at the mouth of the Tippecanoe about 1691; and at Detroit in 1703. The tint is an approximate general area of the Illinois and Michigan counties for those sites, built from whole counties, not a boundary. Wisconsin is text only. The town points are approximate.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · town points approximate

eras.label: 1718–1749 · Kekionga, the Tippecanoe headwaters and Pickawillany
eras.text: Kekionga (Fort Wayne, Allen County, Indiana) was the Miami capital from 1718 to 1794. The Miami were at the Tippecanoe headwaters (Kosciusko County, Indiana) from 1733 to 1751 and at Pickawillany on the Great Miami (Miami County, Ohio) from 1748 to 1752 (Wikipedia). The tint is those counties as whole counties; the two town points are approximate. It is not a boundary.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · town points approximate

eras.label: c.1750–1795 · Wabash divisions: Miami, Wea, Piankashaw
eras.text: Indiana DNR: the Miami proper lived on the upper Wabash around Fort Wayne, the Wea on the central and upper-central Wabash (Ouiatenon), the Piankashaw on the central to lower Wabash near Vincennes. The tint is an approximate general area of that Wabash country, built from whole counties; it is not a boundary. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma names six historical divisions; three survived as separate tribes. After Iroquois pressure emptied the Ohio Valley by the late 1600s, Shawnee, Miami and other Ohio and Indiana peoples extended their hunting back into northern Kentucky in the mid-1700s (Kreinbrink), but permanent villages stayed north of the Ohio. No boundary is given for that hunting ground, so no Kentucky area is drawn.

eras.label: 1791 · Scott and Wilkinson on the Wabash
eras.text: In 1791 Brig. Gen. Charles Scott led about 850 Kentucky mounted volunteers to Ouiatenon (1 June), where Hardin's detachment took 52 prisoners; Wilkinson's 360 men then destroyed the Eel River Miami town of Kenapacomaqua. The Kentucky columns marched north to the tinted Wabash country (approximate general area). Ouiatenon point only; Kenapacomaqua has no sourced coordinates.

eras.label: 1804–1805 · Piankashaw cession and Grouseland
eras.text: 27 Aug 1804 at Vincennes the Piankeshaw ceded the tract between the Ohio and Wabash rivers below Clark’s Grant (the Delawares ceded it on 18 Aug; the Piankashaw had refused to recognise the Delaware title, Art. 5). On 21 Aug 1805 at Grouseland the Miami, Eel River and Wea ceded land south of a line from the Vincennes tract’s north-east corner to the Greenville line 50 miles from the Ohio, and were recognised as joint owners of the Wabash country above the Vincennes tract (the tinted general area). The 1804 tract is hatched as ten Indiana counties, an approximate area; the 1805 line is text only.

eras.label: 1806–1846 · St. Marys (1818) and removal (1846)
eras.text: Wikipedia dates the Treaty of St. Marys to 1818 and the removal of the Miami to 1846. No boundary is sourced for these years, so the tint carries on the earlier general area of the Wabash country (approximate, whole counties, not a boundary).
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area carried forward · no boundary for these years

properties.kind: county list (cession, general area, outside Kentucky)
properties.note: General area only (approximate area, not a boundary). Piankeshaw treaty 27 Aug 1804 Art. 1: 'all that tract of country which lies between the Ohio and Wabash rivers, and below Clark's grant; and the tract called the Vincennes tract ... and a line connecting the said tract and grant, to be drawn parallel to the general course of the road leading from Vincennes to the falls of the Ohio, so as not to pass more than half a mile to the northward of the most northerly bend of said road.' Royce's key (NPS) calls it No. 7, 'in the southern part of the State'. Counties: the ten Indiana counties that lie wholly or almost wholly south of a straight Vincennes-Clarksville chord (Crawford, Dubois, Gibson, Harrison, Perry, Pike, Posey, Spencer, Vanderburgh, Warrick), computed from Census polygons. The real north edge follows the Vincennes road (Buffalo Trace), so county edges are ragged and low-confidence; Clark's Grant (Floyd/Clark area) is excluded. Same tract as in delaware-lenape.json.
Main-map extent: general areas (whole-county shapes, approximate), solid lines in Kentucky and sourced points.

The Wabash valley from Fort Wayne (Kekionga) through Ouiatenon (Lafayette) to Vincennes, the Miami, Wea and Piankashaw country in Indiana DNR and the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma history, as whole counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Wisconsin (Fox River 1654, Wisconsin River 1670–95) is text only. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
